endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: The framework requires identifying and mitigating biases within training data to prevent unequal treatment and ensure consistent outcomes across all patient groups.

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: Healthcare organizations must establish processes to categorize and document the potential risks and biases of health AI tools across relevant domains.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Adverse events, including serious adverse events, should be reported and mitigated consistently, while classifying safety risks by severity and frequency.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: They may additionally wish to allocate risk management resources relative to the severity and likelihood of negative impacts, including where and how these risks manifest, and their direct and material impacts harms in the context of GAI use.

endorsements.title: Operationalizing the EU AI Act in a comprehensive cancer center through an institutional governance framework
endorsements.quote: Classify each tool by data nature and proximity to clinical decision-making before deployment, assigning it to one operational category and to its MDR/AI Act status (Art. 6(1)(b); MDR Rule 11).

endorsements.title: People process technology and operations framework for establishing AI governance in healthcare organizations
endorsements.quote: To support this approach, the committee should establish a standardized process for assessing the risk levels of selected AI products.

endorsements.title: When Is It Safe to Introduce an AI System Into Healthcare? A Practical Decision Algorithm for the Ethical Implementation of Black-Box AI in Medicine
endorsements.quote: Following its risk evaluation, an AI system is categorised as minimal‐risk (i.e., standard use ), moderate‐risk (i.e., innovative use ) or high‐risk (i.e., experimental use ).

endorsements.title: A Pragmatic Framework for Federated Learning Risk and Governance in Academic Medical Centers
endorsements.quote: We note that risk determination (using Table 1 ) is conducted collaboratively by the Artificial Intelligence Governance Committee (AIGC) and the CISO, integrating technical, ethical, and operational expertise to ensure robust, context-sensitive evaluation from the outset.

endorsements.title: Governing Generative AI in Healthcare: A Normative Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Authority, Trust, and the Architecture of Responsibility
endorsements.quote: Tier assignment is an institutional pre-deployment decision.

endorsements.title: Governing Patient-Facing AI-Generated Video in Digital Health: A Risk-and-Ethics Matrix for Deployment, Monitoring, and Change Control
endorsements.quote: On the risk axis, we adapt a hospital-grade matrix consistent with common clinical risk management concepts in which risk reflects the combination of probability and severity.

endorsements.title: Early Online
endorsements.issuer: South African medical journal = Suid-Afrikaanse tydskrif vir geneeskunde
endorsements.quote: A three‑tiered clinical AI risk classification (low, moderate and high) is recommended for Booklet 20 to guide practitioner use, aligned with SAHPRA ’s existing medical‑device categories and consistent with the WHO’s risk‑based approach.

endorsements.title: The VIBE-HI framework: a conceptual model for evaluating vibe coding appropriateness, quality, and safety in health informatics
endorsements.quote: Layer 1 assigns each vibe-coding activity to one of four risk tiers using four criteria: data sensitivity (is PHI involved?), clinical-decision proximity (does the output inform a treatment decision?), user autonomy (can the clinician independently verify the output?), and scale of impact (does the artefact affect an individual or an institution?).

endorsements.title: Mental Health Innovation Is Scaling Faster Than Accountability
endorsements.quote: Tier assignment should occur at market entry based on function as designed, be revisited through change-triggered reassessment whenever models, prompts, interfaces or target populations are materially modified, and be correctable through complaint-triggered functional audit when real-world use demonstrably departs from declared scope.

endorsements.title: When end users can build: AI-assisted application development and the new accountability gap in digital health
endorsements.quote: First, applications should be classified through risk stratification, distinguishing between educational, research, operational, and clinical use cases.

endorsements.title: From Algorithm to Bedside: A Clinician's Framework for AI in Practice
endorsements.quote: Clinicians need a simple mental model for matching oversight to risk ( Box 2 ):

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Should Not Prescribe Alone: A Risk-Stratified Pharmacy Governance Framework for Agentic Clinical Systems
endorsements.quote: Health systems should classify medication-related AI functions by clinical risk and require pharmacist and prescriber review, with stricter controls for therapies involving narrow therapeutic ranges, complex dose individualization or rapid detection of toxicity.

commentary.bottom_line: Thirteen sources endorse classifying each AI use case by risk tier before deployment, but no supplied study tests whether this practice changes the scrutiny high-risk uses receive or reduces harm. No supplied study documents the target hazard either, so the recommendation rests on expert consensus alone.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests pre-deployment risk tiering, and none documents how often high-risk uses receive too little review. Of the listed endorsements, 8 are commentaries and 4 are frameworks or guidance. Expert consensus of this kind cannot be graded as evidence of effect, so no certainty rating for the practice's effect can be assigned.

The endorsing sources propose different schemes. One commentary uses three tiers, VIBE-HI uses four tiers built on four criteria, and another commentary uses a probability-by-severity matrix. No study shows which scheme reviewers apply consistently or how much review time each adds. That gap bears directly on the hazard of inconsistent classification.

Endorsement strength varies across sources. RUAIH guidance states that organizations must categorize and document risks, while NIST AI 600-1 says organizations may scale resources to severity and likelihood. One commentary on mental health AI ties tier assignment to reassessment when models, prompts, interfaces, or target populations change. None of these sources reports outcome data.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should test whether a standardized tiering framework with documented rationale yields consistent tier assignments across reviewers, and whether use cases rated high risk then receive more validation and monitoring. Studies should also measure downstream safety events against a comparison group without structured tiering. Inter-rater agreement studies comparing the three-tier, four-tier, and probability-by-severity schemes would help governance teams choose among them.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is unknown whether tiering criteria account for the added risk an AI tool may carry for these patients. A tool rated low risk for the general population could warrant a higher tier where language access or literacy affects how patients receive its output.
